q-81180.name: Question 1
q-81180.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y=\pi {x}^{2}$ traversed from the point $A(1,\pi )$ to point $B(2,4\pi ),$ then ${\int }_{C}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}})\,dx+3x\,dy=$
q-81180.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=\pi {x}^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+\pi {t}^{2}\,j,\,t\in [1,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2\pi t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}})\,dx+3x\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}})\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+3x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}})\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+3x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi {t}^{2}}{2{t}^{2}})\cdot 1+3t\cdot 2\pi t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+6\pi {t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}1+6\pi {t}^{2}\,dt \\  & =[t+2\pi {t}^{3}]_{1}^{2} \\  & =[2+2\pi (2)^{3}]-[1+2\pi (1)^{3}] \\  & =[2+16\pi ]-[1+2\pi ] \\  & =1+14\pi \end{aligned}
$$

q-90869.name: Question 2
q-90869.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the curve $y={x}^{3}+1$ traversed from the point $A(0,1)$ to point $B(1,2),$ then ${\int }_{C}x\,dx+(y-1)\,dy=$
q-90869.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{3}+1.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+({t}^{3}+1)\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+3{t}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+(y-1)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(y-1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(y-1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\cdot 1+({t}^{3}+1-1)\cdot 3{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t+3{t}^{5}\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{t}^{6}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}]-[0] \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

q-124653.name: Question 3
q-124653.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}({e}^{x}+y)\,dx-x\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(0,\sqrt{3})$ to the point $B(-\sqrt{3},0).$
q-124653.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is a circle of radius $\sqrt{3}$ centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({e}^{x}+y)\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }({e}^{x}+y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(({e}^{x}+y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}-x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }({e}^{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}-3{sin}^{2}⁡t-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}-3\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+3\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=3cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,t∈[π2,π]

q-124661.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(x+y)\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=36$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $(0,3)$ to the point $(-2,0).$
q-124661.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $3,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & ={x}^{′}(t)\,i+{y}^{′}(t)\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(x+y)\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(x-y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(x+y)\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }((x-y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+(x+y)\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+6{sin}^{2}⁡t+6{cos}^{2}⁡t+9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+6\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+6t]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =[(-\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )+6\pi )-(-\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+3\pi )] \\  & =(-\frac{5}{4}+6\pi )-(\frac{5}{4}+3\pi ) \\  & =3\pi -\frac{5}{2} \\  & =\frac{6\pi -5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate ∫C(x−y)dx+(x+y)dy, where C is part of the ellipse 9x2+4y2=36 traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point (0,3) to the point (−2,0).

a
 6π
b
 3π
c

d
 5π+14

6π−52

Correct
EXPLANATION

Since C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 2 and 3, respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=2cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,t∈[π2,π]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=x′(t)i+y′(t)j=−2sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj.

We can now evaluate the line integral:

∫C(x−y)dx+(x+y)dy=∫π/2π(x−y)dxdtdt+(x+y)dydtdt=∫π/2π((x−y)dxdt+(x+y)dydt)dt=∫π/2π(2cos⁡t−3sin⁡t)⋅(−2sin⁡t)+(2cos⁡t+3sin⁡t)⋅3cos⁡tdt=∫π/2π(−4cos⁡tsin⁡t+6sin2⁡t+6cos2⁡t+9cos⁡tsin⁡t)dt=∫π/2π5sin⁡tcos⁡t+6dt=∫π/2π52sin⁡2t+6dt=[−54cos⁡2t+6t]π/2π=[(−54cos⁡(2π)+6π)−(−54cos⁡(π)+3π)]=(−54+6π)−(54+3π)=3π−52=6π−52

q-124664.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y=2\sqrt{x}$ traversed from the point $P(1,2)$ to point $Q(4,4),$ then ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(x+y)\,dy=$
q-124664.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=2\sqrt{x}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j={t}^{2}\,i+2t\,j,\,t\in [1,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2t\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(x+y)\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(x-y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(x+y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}((x-y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x+y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-2t)\cdot 2t+({t}^{2}+2t)\cdot 2\,dt \\  & =2{\int }_{1}^{2}t({t}^{2}-2t)+({t}^{2}+2t)\,dt \\  & =2{\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+2t\,dt \\  & =2{[\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}+{t}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2[(\frac{{2}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{2}^{3}}{3}+{2}^{2})-(\frac{{1}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{1}^{3}}{3}+{1}^{2})] \\  & =2[4-\frac{8}{3}+4-\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{3}-1] \\  & =2\cdot \frac{53}{12} \\  & =\frac{53}{6}\end{aligned}
$$
